name: Juche
info: Juche, the Juche idea, is the official ideology of North Korea and its ruling Workers' Party of Korea; it stresses human independence and consciousness, national self-reliance and loyalty to the leader, and it took shape from 1955 under Kim Il Sung.

facts.thinkers: Kim Il Sung, to whom North Korean sources attribute it; Hwang Jang-yop, his top adviser on philosophy, whom Western scholars generally credit with its conceptualization and early development; Kim Jong Il, who declared it a distinct ideology in the 1970s and developed it further; Kim Jong Un, who succeeded him
facts.texts: Kim Il Sung's speech “On Eliminating Dogmatism and Formalism and Establishing Juche in Ideological Work” (1955), the “Juche speech”; his 1967 speech to the Supreme People's Assembly on independence, self-sustenance and self-defence; the Ten Principles for the Establishment of a Monolithic Ideological System (1974); Kim Jong Il's On the Juche Idea (1982)
facts.ideas: the masses of the people as the masters of the revolution and its motive force; political independence (chaju); economic self-sufficiency (charip); military self-reliance (chawi); the primacy of ideology and political consciousness; the leader at the centre of the masses (suryong); opposition to reliance on great powers (sadae)
facts.today: It is the official ideology of North Korea and the Workers' Party of Korea, in the form of Kimilsungism–Kimjongilism until the party's 9th Congress in 2026 removed that name from its rules; abroad it has been adopted or studied by small parties and groups, such as the Nepal Workers' and Peasants' Party

t: Juche holds that the masses of the people are the masters of the revolution and that a country prospers once it achieves political, economic and military self-reliance, which North Korea's government pursued from the 1950s.

Kim Il Sung's 1955 speech on establishing Juche in ideological work was a purge of dogmatism, and the 1956 failed challenge to his leadership led to a purge of pro-Soviet and pro-Chinese elements from the party.

Scholars disagree about what Juche is: Brian Reynolds Myers likens it to Japanese fascism and ultranationalism, Charles K. Armstrong calls it a quasi-religion, and Derek R. Ford stresses its continuity with Marxism–Leninism.
dyk: Juche was a word of German philosophy before it was a doctrine: it was coined in Japan in 1887 to translate Subjekt, and North Korean editions of Marx used it even before 1955. The Juche calendar counts years from 1912, the year of Kim Il Sung's birth.
ev: Kim Il Sung gives the “Juche speech”, the first documented reference to Juche as an ideology
A failed challenge to Kim Il Sung's leadership leads to a purge of pro-Soviet and pro-Chinese elements from the Workers' Party of Korea
In Indonesia Kim Il Sung gives the speech that Andrei Lankov takes as the first reference to Juche as an ideology
Kim Jong Il introduces Kimilsungism and the Ten Principles for the Establishment of a Monolithic Ideological System
North Korea begins organizing international seminars on Juche, the first in Antananarivo, Madagascar
On the Juche Idea is published under Kim Jong Il's name
Kim Jong Il introduces Socialism of Our Style after the revolutions that brought down the Eastern Bloc
The Juche calendar is adopted, counting years from 1912

sections.origins:
Official statements by the North Korean government attribute the origin of Juche to Kim Il Sung's experiences in the Down-with-Imperialism Union during Korea's liberation struggle against Japan. The first documented reference to Juche as an ideology dates to 1955, when Kim Il Sung delivered a speech titled “On Eliminating Dogmatism and Formalism and Establishing Juche in Ideological Work”. The speech promoted a political purge similar to the Yan'an Rectification Movement in China and became known as the “Juche speech”.

The word comes from the Sino-Japanese 主體, coined in 1887 to translate the concept of Subjekt in German philosophy into Japanese. It migrated to Korean around the turn of the century with that meaning and appeared in Japanese translations of Karl Marx. North Korean editions of Marx used the word even before it was attributed to Kim Il Sung in its supposedly novel meaning in 1955.

Western scholars generally agree that Hwang Jang-yop, Kim Il Sung's top adviser on philosophy, was responsible for the conceptualization and early development of Juche. Hwang rediscovered the speech in the late 1950s, when Kim Il Sung, having established a cult of personality, sought to develop his own version of Marxism–Leninism and solidify his position in the Workers' Party of Korea. Andrei Lankov argues that the first reference to Juche as an ideology came on 14 April 1965, in a speech Kim gave in Indonesia, and that the 1955 speech used the word in a different meaning.
sections.ideas:
According to Naenara, North Korea's official web portal, Juche means that the masses of the people are the masters of the revolution and construction and also its motive force. It incorporates the historical materialist ideas of Marxism–Leninism but emphasizes human agency, the role of political consciousness and the primacy of ideology and propaganda. Its goal is a self-reliant state that determines its political, economic and military affairs independently.

Three principles carry this goal. Political independence (chaju) means equality and mutual respect among nations and the right of every state to self-determination; it is set against sadaejuui, reliance on a great power, though Juche does not advocate total isolation and encourages cooperation between socialist states. Economic self-sufficiency (charip) is held to be required for political independence; in On the Juche Idea Kim Jong Il argued for an independent national economy based on heavy industry. Military self-reliance (chawi) calls for a domestic defence industry, and Kim Jong Il held that allies' military aid is effective only if the state is strong in its own right.

The theory of Suryong makes the leader central. Where Marxism–Leninism sees the material conditions of production as the driving force of history, Juche takes human beings to be the driving force, but holds that the masses need the leadership of a great leader. Its summary is that the popular masses are placed in the centre of everything and the leader is the centre of the masses. The theory describes the leader as a flawless human being who never makes mistakes.
sections.spread:
Juche was first regarded as a variant of Marxism–Leninism. In the 1970s Kim Jong Il declared it a distinct ideology, and as he emerged as Kim Il Sung's likely successor loyalty to the leader was increasingly emphasized, as expressed in the Ten Principles for the Establishment of a Monolithic Ideological System, introduced in 1974 together with Kimilsungism. Kim Jong Il said in 1976 that Marxism–Leninism had become obsolete and that Kimilsungism could not be explained within its frameworks.

In the 1980s and 1990s Kim Jong Il made further breaks from Marxism–Leninism while insisting that Juche inherits it. In 1982 he stated that love for the nation came before love for socialism, and in 1990 he introduced Socialism of Our Style. Songun, military-first politics, was first mentioned in 1997 and credited to Kim Jong Il as the next stage of Juche; in late 2021 Kim Jong Un declared that it would be replaced by “people-first politics”. After Kim Jong Il's death in December 2011 Kimilsungism became Kimilsungism–Kimjongilism, adopted in April 2012 as the party's only guiding idea.

Outside Korea Kim Il Sung promoted Juche in the Third World as an anti-imperialist ideology. The first International Scientific Seminar on the Juche Idea met in Antananarivo from 28 to 30 September 1976, with participants from more than 50 countries, and in 1978 North Korea founded the International Institute of the Juche Idea in Tokyo. Juche study groups formed abroad, and in South Korea a faction of the student movements of the 1980s, the Juche faction or Jusapa, embraced it as an alternative to the country's political system.
sections.power:
Juche has been the official ideology of North Korea and its ruling party. After the devastation of the Korean War the state rebuilt its economy on heavy industry, aiming at the greatest possible self-sufficiency, and developed what has been called the most autarkic industrial economy in the world. It received aid and technical assistance from the Soviet Union and China but did not join Comecon. In the 1990s it had one of the lowest rates of dependence on petroleum, using hydroelectric power and coal, and its textile industry used vinylon, called the “Juche fiber”, made from local coal and limestone. The Korean People's Army is one of the largest on earth and has developed its own nuclear missiles.

In politics, North Korea opposed what it saw as Soviet and Chinese attempts to interfere in its postwar affairs. A failed challenge to Kim Il Sung's leadership in 1956 led to a purge of pro-Soviet and pro-Chinese elements from the party. North Korea rejected Khrushchev's de-Stalinization but avoided taking sides in the Sino-Soviet split, was admitted to the Non-Aligned Movement in 1975 and presented itself as a leader of the Third World. As the Eastern Bloc collapsed and introduced market reforms, North Korea emphasized Juche more in both theory and practice.

Commentators have often pointed to the discrepancy between self-sufficiency and North Korea's dependence on foreign aid, especially in its economic crisis of the 1990s. The pursuit of autarky has been blamed for contributing to the crisis: attempts at self-sufficiency led to inefficiency and to the neglect of export opportunities in industries with a comparative advantage. In 1997 the government adopted the Juche calendar.
sections.critiques:
Critics have called Juche a nationalist ideology and a departure from Marxism–Leninism. Brian Reynolds Myers argues that it has more in common with Japanese fascism and ultranationalism than with Marxism–Leninism. Suh Dae-sook argues that Kim Il Sung did not explain the difference between socialist patriotism, which he supported, and nationalism, which he opposed. Charles K. Armstrong holds that North Korea may appear “Stalinist in form” but is “nationalist in content”, and Shin Gi-wook that its government stresses the Korean people's blood, soul and national traits, supports social hierarchy rather than a classless society, and places ideology above materialism. Derek R. Ford, by contrast, emphasizes its continuity with Marxism–Leninism and credits it as the principle that let North Korea survive the collapse of the Eastern Bloc.

A few critics dismiss the idea that Juche is an ideology at all. Myers says it has no underlying belief system and exists to be praised and not read; Alzo David-West calls it “meaningless on logical and naturalistic grounds”; Robert E. Kelly argues that it exists solely to protect the Kim family's monopoly over political power. Felix Abt, who lived in North Korea, calls Myers's arguments “shaky”, and Bruce Cumings and Christoph Hartmut Bluth argue that it is an ideal of self-reliance that North Korea has tried to implement.

Armstrong calls Juche a quasi-religion and argues that familism became a political religion in it, with Kim Il Sung as the father of the people; Byung Ho Chung and Heonik Kwon liken the commemorations of the Kim leaders to Confucian ancestor worship. Western Marxists have called the cult of personality non-Marxist and undemocratic.
sections.legacy:
Juche remains the official ideology of North Korea. Kimilsungism–Kimjongilism, which the party's 4th Conference of April 2012 declared its only guiding idea, was removed from the Rules of the Workers' Party of Korea at the 9th Congress in 2026. North Korea's official portal describes the state as independent and socialist, guided by Kimilsungism–Kimjongilism.

Juche has been taken up outside North Korea. The Black Panther Party of the United States studied it in the 1960s and 1970s. In 2014 the secretary-general of the Nigerian–DPRK Friendship Association, Alhassan Mamman Muhammed, claimed there were thousands of adherents in Nigeria, and the Nepal Workers' and Peasants' Party declared Juche its guiding idea in 2016. Far-left and far-right organisations have adopted or studied it, among them, reportedly, a neo-Nazi group and the Rural People's Party, an affiliate of the Order of Nine Angles. The Albanian leader Enver Hoxha called Kim Il Sung's attempts to spread Juche in the Third World “pretensions”.

Comparisons have been drawn with other doctrines. Park Sang-seek finds rhetorical similarities with Syrian Ba'athism, though Juche has in his view a stronger ideological basis. Benjamin Zycher wrote that the political ideology of Donald Trump shares with Juche a policy of isolationism and autarky. Its concept of a sacred leader has been compared to the State Shinto of Imperial Japan, in which the Emperor was seen as a divine being.

summary: Juche, the Juche idea, is the official ideology of North Korea, first documented in Kim Il Sung's 1955 speech. It holds that the masses are masters of the revolution and that a state must be politically, economically and militarily self-reliant, and it gives the leader a central role. Scholars dispute whether it is Marxism, nationalism or a quasi-religion.
notes: Start 1955, circa true: the article gives the 1955 speech as the first documented reference; Andrei Lankov places the first reference to Juche as an ideology in 1965 and says the 1955 speech used the word in a different meaning. Both are given in the text.

The article says nothing of famine, camps, executions or death tolls under Juche rule, and gives no figures for repression beyond the 1956 purge of pro-Soviet and pro-Chinese elements. I wrote only what it says; the editor may want a second source for the record in power (the 1990s crisis is described only as an economic crisis).

The article contradicts itself slightly on who attributed the word: it says the word was attributed to Kim Il Sung in its novel meaning in 1955, while Lankov dates the ideology to 1965. Both are reported.
The 2026 removal of Kimilsungism–Kimjongilism from the party rules is as the article states it; the 'today' fact repeats it. Gregorian year 2026 is called Juche 115 in the article; not used.
The article has no reference list or further reading in the saved text, so references is empty.

Left out: the Arirang Festival and ritual passages, the Songun details of the 1999 editorial, military technical details (UDMH, engines, CNC counts), the neo-Nazi organisations other than one reported affiliate, and Hwang Jang-yop's rewriting of Korean communist history.
